title: Paneer Lababdar, Millet Pulao and Mulberry Phirni: What BRICS Leaders Ate at Modi's Gala Dinner
excerpt: A ten-course vegetarian banquet at Bharat Mandapam took world leaders from Gujarati khandvi to Himalayan morels to mulberry-topped phirni — with millets front and centre.
body:
• Prime Minister Narendra Modi hosted a vegetarian gala dinner at Bharat Mandapam on Saturday, the opening day of the 18th BRICS Summit, serving an elaborate multi-course menu to world leaders including China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin.
  • The menu blended regional Indian cuisines with contemporary plating: khandvi mille-feuille and khumb galouti starters, a six-dish main course built around paneer lababdar, Himalayan morel mushrooms and millet pulao, and desserts pairing Old Delhi fruit cream with shahtoot phirni.
  • Millets featured prominently, continuing the government's push to position the coarse grain as a global superfood since the International Year of Millets in 2023.
  • The dinner was accompanied by a cultural programme with more than 100 artistes drawn from India and other BRICS member countries.

The leaders of some of the world's largest emerging economies sat down to a very Indian table in New Delhi on Saturday. Prime Minister Narendra Modi hosted a gala dinner at Bharat Mandapam on the opening day of the 18th BRICS Summit, laying out a vegetarian banquet that moved from Gujarat to Lucknow to Tamil Nadu in a single sitting.

The dinner, attended by leaders and delegates including Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, was a ten-course affair spanning starters, a six-dish main course and dessert, with at least two choices per course alongside freshly made breads, according to reports on the menu published by Indian media.

Starters: Khandvi goes French, mushrooms go Lucknowi

The meal opened with Khandvi Mille-Feuille — a steamed gram-flour roll tempered with mustard, coconut and curry leaves, served with kesar mango, micro-greens and a yoghurt dressing. The dish takes a humble Gujarati snack and rebuilds it in the layered style of a French pastry. It was followed by Khumb Galouti: tender pan-grilled mushroom kebabs paired with mint pearls and served on sheermal bread, a vegetarian turn on the celebrated galouti kebab of Lucknow.

"The dish takes a humble Gujarati snack and rebuilds it in the layered style of a French pastry."

Main course: a tour of India's regions

The centrepiece of the evening was the main course, which stitched together cooking traditions from the Himalayas to the south. Paneer Lababdar, cottage cheese simmered in a rich shallot-and-tomato gravy, anchored the spread. Beside it sat Gucchi Marmik, made with Himalayan morel mushrooms and asparagus simmered with saffron, raisins and mamra almonds — a dish that carries the high-altitude flavours of the mountain ranges into a banquet setting.

From the south came Carrot Bean Poriyal, with carrots and green beans tossed in South Indian spices, hand-pressed virgin coconut oil and fresh coconut, and Thakkali Belle Saaru, a light lentil broth of toor dal, tomatoes and curry leaves. Millet Pulao — basmati rice cooked with pearl millet, spices and seasonal aromatics — sat alongside Beetroot Raita and an assortment of Indian breads.

The inclusion of millets was deliberate. The Indian government has championed the coarse grain as a nutritious, climate-resilient alternative to rice and wheat ever since it led the UN-backed International Year of Millets in 2023, and putting millet pulao on the plates of world leaders is food diplomacy of the most direct kind.

Dessert and the cultural evening

Dessert paired street-food heritage with classical sweets. Old Delhi Fruit Cream with Jalebi combined seasonal fruits and lightly whipped cream with the crisp traditional fritter, while Shahtoot Phirni — a slow-cooked milk-and-rice pudding topped with fresh mulberries and edible gold leaf — offered a more courtly finish. Beverages stayed non-alcoholic and tropical: pomegranate juice and coconut water, described on the menu as "a stream of refreshing flavours."

The dinner was accompanied by a cultural performance featuring an ensemble of more than 100 artistes, drawn mainly from India as well as other BRICS member countries, with a special BRICS symphony performance among the highlights of the evening.

Food as statecraft

Modi's government has made culinary diplomacy a signature of its summit hosting. The BRICS banquet follows the pattern set during India's G20 presidency, when state dinners leaned heavily on millet-based dishes and regional specialities to project India as both ancient and modern. Entirely vegetarian, regionally pan-Indian, and printed in both English and Hindi, the menu told a story about how India wants to be seen: confident in its own traditions, fluent in global form, and eager to feed the conversation.

The 18th BRICS Summit, hosted by India in the national capital on September 12 and 13, brings together leaders of the emerging-economy bloc to discuss cooperation and the voice of the Global South in international institutions.
image_caption: BRICS leaders, including Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin, seated at the gala dinner at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi. The menu highlighted millet-based dishes and regional Indian ingredients, including paneer lababdar and mulberry phirni.
nri_angle: The gala dinner menu showcases regional Indian cuisine on the world stage, a point of cultural pride for the diaspora, and continues India's millet diplomacy that diaspora food writers have been tracking since 2023.
author: Diaspora Desk
